stories.headline: ‘Felt like an earthquake’: Neighbours recount after building collapse in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar
stories.title: ‘Felt like an earthquake’: Neighbours recount after building collapse in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar
stories.summary: While one resident felt violent tremors and rushed out of her home, others learnt of the collapse from blaring ambulance sirens and frantic cries for help in Chawri Bazaar
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'building collapse' in title weight 46
article_sentences: The residents in Old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar have recalled tremors and sirens as a building collapses.
“I was sitting on my bed when I suddenly felt strong jerks and vibrations.
It felt like an earthquake had struck.
I immediately jumped off the bed and rushed out of my room.
I asked my husband if he had felt it too, but he said he hadn’t.
I checked with others, but nobody seemed to have felt anything.
I let it be, only to later discover that a building had collapsed right next door,” said Soha Ali, who has lived in an adjacent building for the past 35 years.
She said she had been noticing construction workers moving in and out of the building over the past few months.
Another woman living in the neighbourhood, who did not wish to be identified, said she was alerted to the incident by the sound of ambulance sirens and the commotion outside.
“I did not feel any vibrations, but when I heard the sirens and people rushing about, I stepped out to find out what had happened and asked my neighbours,” she said.
Having moved into the neighbourhood only three months ago, she said the incident had left her apprehensive about the safety of buildings in the area.
Several residents said the collapse itself was not immediately audible to many in the neighbourhood, as the building was located deep inside a narrow, congested lane.

stories.headline: India-made Mercedes for global markets? A matter of when, not if, says group CEO
stories.title: India-made Mercedes for global markets? A matter of when, not if, says group CEO
stories.summary: Mercedes-Benz Group CEO Ola Källenius has said the German luxury carmaker will deepen its engineering and component-sourcing presence in India, and that building cars here for exports is a matter of “when, not if”.“[I’m an] India believer, and certainly an India optimist,” Källenius, who was in Pune on Wednesday for the launch of the electric GLC, said at a select media roundtable.The remarks come as India’s largest luxury carmaker heads for its best year in the country even as competition from BMW intensifies.Asked whether India could become an export base, Källenius said: “…that is more a question of when, as opposed to a question of if, but I want to make [it] clear: We have not made such a decision at this point in time.”India is expected to sell about 5 million vehicles this fiscal, but the premium luxury segment is only a little over 1 percent, or roughly 60,000 cars.Selling around 20,000 of them gives Mercedes a one-third share of that pool. “That’s great news… 33 percent market share. But that is absolutely not the end of the journey for Mercedes-Benz in India.”Also Read: You can’t become Formula One world champion without India: Mercedes CEOThe first step is organic growth as the economy expands over the next five to seven years, he said. A full-vehicle export programme would depend on finding a price point in the market, and a product in the portfolio to match it, that justifies the investment. “That point, we don’t know yet when it is,” he said. “We have not made such a decision at this point in time.”Components might be sourced from India before any fully built car is. “We are building strong tech and supply relationships in India, not just for India but also for the rest of the world,” he said. “We can export out of India on a component basis before you ask the question on a full vehicle.”The CEO welcomed the free trade agreement being put in place between the European Union and India. Less friction makes export transactions “in any direction” more likely, said Källenius, president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association.Doubling DownEarlier in the day, while launching the electric GLC at its plant in Pune’s Chakan, Källenius said the carmaker is “doubling down [on India]”.Asked what doubling down means for a company that already has a large R&D centre—the largest outside of Germany—and about 95 percent localisation, Källenius told Forbes India there are several legs to it, first of which is R&D.Mercedes-Benz Research and Development India (MBRDI), which turns 30 this year, started as a small team that took tasks from “mission control” in Germany and sent them back, he said.Also Read: Mercedes-Benz will bring plug-in hybrids to India: MD Santosh IyerThe company now wants what he called “R&D global”, a full integration with engineering hubs elsewhere.India now has mechanical, electrical, powertrain, software and AI skills, he said. “We are talking about the absolute frontier of technological development.” He said MBRDI is on “eye level” with the group’s centres in Germany.The second leg is the supply base.India’s component makers are growing more sophisticated, and Mercedes can use them for more than local content.Many of Mercedes’ supplier partnerships, European, American, Japanese, Korean and increasingly Chinese, are worldwide relationships and not confined to one region.“So that’s a part of the doubling down. Then grow organically and then ultimately when the market comes to that point, find a point where you can take the bigger step at some point in time.”Källenius declined to put a number on India’s longer-term importance. “I don’t want to create the headline prematurely,” he said, before adding that India’s weight in the company’s thinking would be “higher tomorrow than today”.Also Read: Can Mercedes-Benz Stay Ahead as BMW Closes In?Going ElectricThe Electric GLC it launched Wednesday starts at Rs 78.5 lakh and is sold out, with 1,000 bookings already received.The CLA electric sedan, its most affordable electric car yet with a price tag of Rs 55 lakh, is also sold out. It was launched in April this year.The robust response comes as the country’s EV market gains momentum across the board, with uncertainty triggered by the Iran war prompting more consumers to consider switching to electric mobility.“India is going electric,” Källenius said on Wednesday.He expects EVs to account for a high single-digit share of Mercedes’ India sales this year and a double-digit share next year, “probably starting with a two”. Mercedes’ current EV penetration is around 14 percent.He cited factors such as increasing range and features like pre-cooling the cabin before getting in as drivers of EV interest. Higher petrol prices and sentiment help, but “fundamentals reside in the product”.Källenius, however, was clear that a fully electric market is still far off.Mercedes Benz has bet on a multi-powertrain strategy, unlike BMW, which is going big on electric.In 2020, Mercedes said it would be ready to serve the market fully electrically by the end of the decade, where market conditions allow. The first wave of EVs came in below expectations, he said, but the company was not discouraged. It is now in the first 12 to 18 months of what he called a second generation of electric cars.The combustion engine will stay “for minimum 10, probably 15 years”, he said. The whole combustion line-up has been updated to the Euro 7 emissions standard, including the V8, which he said makes Mercedes the first manufacturer to do so.On diesel, he said Mercedes’ latest engines are the cleanest it has built and remain a strong option for people who cover 60,000-70,000 km a year. “It will stay in the portfolio for the foreseeable future,” he said, adding that cheaper fuel in India makes the case stronger here.Asked whether India would see more EVs than previously planned, he said: “Every meaningful portfolio position where we see a chance in India will come to India.”Also Read: All cars from Mercedes starting this year are E25-compliant: MD‘Right Idea, Wrong Method’Asked about turmoil in Germany’s car industry, Källenius said the sector is in the middle of a disruption driven by the road to zero emissions and by an “intelligence revolution” in software, sensors and AI. Unlike the move from the BlackBerry to the iPhone, this is a 20- to 25-year industrial transition.He listed several problems at once. China’s market, long the growth engine, has gone from rising to flat to falling, setting off price pressure that has cut profitability. Tariffs hit earnings last year because Mercedes is “probably the biggest industrial exporter to the United States”. The war in Ukraine is in its fourth year, and a conflict in West Asia is pushing up oil prices. “So now you have a cocktail for a really fun job,” he said.On European regulation, speaking in his role at ACEA, he said the industry accepts the destination of zero emissions but disagrees with the route. “Right idea, wrong method,” he said.Policymakers should move from an approach built on statistics and planning to one that leaves more to the market, and some rules are likely to be revised in the final phase of the policy debate.He said Mercedes can ride this out. “We have a very strong balance sheet. Our company is industrially debt-free. Our pension obligations are all financed with more than 100 percent and we have €30 billion net industrial liquidity. So we can enter into this tough battle, as it will be, but from a position of strength and with some strategic patience.”Top-end vehicles make up about 15 percent of Mercedes’ global sales but generate more than 40 percent of contribution, he said. The company’s share of that segment in India is over 20 percent.

stories.title: Delhi building collapse: AAP alleges rampant corruption; BJP MP blames builder greed

article_sentences: The building collapse in old Delhi’s Chawri Bazar triggered a political war of words, with the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) accusing the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government of “rampant extortion” and “corruption”.
“The Rekha Gupta government and the MCD [Municipal Corporation of Delhi] have conducted multiple safety audits of buildings across Delhi, yet buildings continue to collapse.
Safety audits have been ordered repeatedly, but instead of taking concrete action, multiple departments have collected bribes.
This is why buildings collapse every month,” AAP Delhi president Saurabh Bharadwaj wrote on X.
The party demanded that the government order a high-level inquiry into the incident and take strict action against the officials responsible.
Meanwhile, officials said that CM Rekha Gupta, along with East Delhi MP and State BJP president Harsh Malhotra, reached the spot to take stock soon after receiving news about the collapse.
Speaking to reporters, Mr. Malhotra said, “At first glance, this appears to be a case of extreme greed.
It seems the building owner and contractor wanted to erect the building overnight before the anti-pollution restrictions came into force.”

“In Matia Mahal and Ballimaran constituencies, under the Self-Certification Scheme, maps are being passed, and five- to seven-storey buildings are being raised overnight with half-baked raw and concrete slabs under local political patronage.
This is extremely dangerous,” said Delhi BJP spokesperson Praveen Shankar Kapoor.
He added that the MCD Commissioner should order regular inspection of maps passed under the scheme.
“In this building, two slabs were laid in just 11 days, and the third was being prepared today [Thursday], which led to the accident.

stories.headline: Centre tells Supreme Court it may set up a panel to review UGC equity on campus regulations
stories.title: Centre tells Supreme Court it may set up a panel to review UGC equity on campus regulations
stories.summary: The Centre said it was examining criticism about the Regulations, which had sparked protests by upper-caste student groups; the Court had stayed the regulations in January, stating that they were “too vague”
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Union government is “contemplating” having a special committee review the University Grants Commission (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026, it said in a submission to the Supreme Court on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The Regulations were intended to fight discrimination within educational campuses, but had triggered protests by upper caste students claiming that the rules were one-sided.

In a brief hearing before a Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, for the government, sought more time to come back with a comprehensive response, but added that the Centre was examining criticism about the 2026 Regulations.
“The government is contemplating a special committee to relook the UGC Regulations,” Mr. Mehta submitted.
In January 2026, the top court had stayed the Regulations, finding them “too sweeping” and vague.
It had ordered that the University Grants Commission (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2012, would continue to be in force.
The Court had further issued notice to the government and the University Grants Commission (UGC) on separate petitions challenging Regulation 3(c) of the 2026 Regulations.

These petitions had argued that the provision defined ‘caste-based discrimination’ in a narrow manner, limiting its ambit only to prejudice shown against members of the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and Other Backward Classes.

The stimulus behind the 2026 Regulations was a petition filed jointly by the mothers of Rohith Vemula and Payal Tadvi in the Supreme Court against “rampant” caste discrimination in higher education institutions.

Vemula, a PhD scholar at Hyderabad Central University, and Tadvi, a tribal student of the TN Topiwala National Medical College, died by suicide in January 2016 and May 2019, respectively, after being subject to on-campus caste bias.
Senior advocate Indira Jaising and advocate Prasanna S., appearing for both mothers, had intervened against the Court’s January stay order.
They had argued that keeping the Regulations in abeyance was akin to “calling a fully-abled person disabled”.

stories.headline: Cabinet approves 30-year lease of four acres in High Grounds to Bangalore Turf Club
stories.title: Cabinet approves 30-year lease of four acres in High Grounds to Bangalore Turf Club
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet approves' in title weight 44
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: With the racing activity held by the Bangalore Turf Club (BTC) expected to be relocated to Kunigal, the State government on Thursday approved the leasing of four acres on the current premises in High Grounds to the BTC for a period of 30 years.
The four-acre area currently houses the club facilities and includes a heritage structure.
While agreeing to shift racing activities to the Kunigal Stud Farm, the BTC had sought six acres to continue its club activities and off-course betting centre.
However, the government agreed to provide four acres.
Rural Development and Panchayat Raj Minister Eshwar Khandre told presspersons after the Cabinet meeting that the government had approved the lease proposal.
“The club has also sought some time to relocate the racing activities to Kunigal,” he said.
The development follows an earlier decision by the State government not to extend the lease term to the BTC and its offer of land to build a racecourse at the Kunigal Stud Farm.
After initial reluctance, the BTC agreed to shift activities to Kunigal while seeking six acres to continue club operations and its off-course betting centre on the existing premises.
Mr. Khandre also announced that the winter session at Belagavi, scheduled to be held from November 30 to December 11, has been rescheduled to start from December 2.

article_sentences: The State Cabinet has approved an additional ₹1,118 crore to complete the 134-km road project connecting Attibele, Sarjapur, Dommasandra, Gunjur, Varthur, Whitefield, the Kempegowda International Airport and Nelamangala, Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda said.
The project, sanctioned in 2017, was initially estimated to cost ₹2,290 crore.
However, the revised project cost has increased to ₹3,409 crore owing to changes during implementation, higher land acquisition costs, rising prices, delays, and additional works.

The additional funds are expected to accelerate construction along the road, particularly in the Gunjur–Varthur stretch in east Bengaluru, where commuters have been facing traffic congestion and inconvenience due to ongoing infrastructure works and poor road conditions.
In a statement, Mr. Gowda thanked Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar and the Cabinet for approving the additional allocation.
He said the Cabinet had also expressed displeasure over the delays and instructed officials to ensure early completion of the project.

The Minister said he had sought a proposal from the Public Works Department (PWD) for additional funds following his field inspection of the road, after the condition of Varthur Kodi and Sarjapur Road drew widespread criticism.
School buses travelling on the feeder roads to this stretch were stuck for over two hours last month.
The upgrading of SH-35 was taken up in 2019, setting the deadline to 2021.
The project includes building a flyover at Varthur Kodi and widening the stretch between Varthur Kodi and the Varthur-Sarjapur stretch.

opening: The State Cabinet has approved an additional ₹1,118 crore to complete the 134-km road project connecting Attibele, Sarjapur, Dommasandra, Gunjur, Varthur, Whitefield, the Kempegowda International Airport and Nelamangala, Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda said.
The project, sanctioned in 2017, was initially estimated to cost ₹2,290 crore.
body: However, the revised project cost has increased to ₹3,409 crore owing to changes during implementation, higher land acquisition costs, rising prices, delays, and additional works.

bullets.text: The additional funds are expected to accelerate construction along the road, particularly in the Gunjur–Varthur stretch in east Bengaluru, where commuters have been facing traffic congestion and inconvenience due to ongoing infrastructure works and poor road conditions.
